tagline.text: The Aklan provincial museum on the site of a Spanish-era schoolhouse, next to Kalibo Cathedral

location.label: Location
location.text: 11 Martelino Street, Kalibo, Aklan, next to Pastrana Park and Kalibo Cathedral

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱50~300 (per person, entrance fee and downtown tricycle)

children.text: Museo it Akean is the Aklan provincial museum beside Pastrana Park in Kalibo. It opened as a museum in 1980 in a school building put up by Spanish authorities in 1882, and it displays Aklan's geography, history, food, crafts and local figures.

Museo it Akean, whose name means "Museum of Aklan" in the Aklanon language, is a provincial museum at 11 Martelino Street in Kalibo, right next to Kalibo Cathedral on the edge of Pastrana Park. The building is a two-story structure put up by Spanish authorities in 1882, and it was first a school called Escuelahan it Hari, meaning "the King's School." Children from Kalibo and the neighboring town attended, and during the war it is said to have served as a garrison. It became a museum in 1980. The Philstar lifestyle section gives 1822 as the year the same building was put up, so the dates disagree.

An earthquake in the mid-1980s badly damaged the century-old building, and today only part of the original pediment survives. A flagpole stands on top of it, and visitors can pose with the pediment on the top floor. The exhibits run through geography, pre-colonial and colonial history, Aklan's people and cuisine, art and cultural heritage, social progress, crafts and economy, and Kalibo's tourism industry. Some exhibits also present old claims that scholars have shown to be fabricated. On the mezzanine of the main staircase hangs a painting of the "Calivo" baptism scene.

The museum also has galleries about people from Aklan. Gabriel M. Reyes, born in Kalibo in 1892, was the first Filipino Archbishop of Manila and served from 1949 until his death in 1952, and the nonprofit that runs the museum bears his name. Jaime Cardinal Sin, from New Washington next to Kalibo, was Archbishop of Manila during the People Power revolutions of 1986 and 2001. Godofredo P. Ramos, who wrote the 1956 law creating the province of Aklan, is called the "Father of Aklan," and Caticlan Airport, the gateway to Boracay, is named after him. There are also galleries on World War II guerrilla heroes Capt. Gil Mijares and Col. Pastor Martelino.

Aklan became its own province in 1956. After the Spanish left Kalibo in late December 1898 the Americans came to Panay, and in 1901 a civil government was set up with Aklan as a district of Capiz. In 1956 President Ramon Magsaysay signed the law creating the province, and Aklan separated. A walk through the museum summarizes at a glance why Kalibo is a city of the Ati-Atihan festival and faith and how Aklan grew into a province of its own. It suits the start of a city walk or a short indoor outing. The Philstar lifestyle section (2022) said you could cover the museum, Pastrana Park, snacks from the Sunday market (kakanin at about
each) and Tigayon Hill for about
, mostly entrance fees. That excludes flights and lodging, and prices may have gone up, so treat it only as a guide.
Spanish authorities put up this building in 1882 and called it the "King's School." An earthquake destroyed most of it, but the pediment remains, and on the top floor you can pose with the flagpole.
Exhibits explaining pre-colonial and colonial history run throughout the building. Some old claims that scholars have shown to be fabricated are presented as well, so read the labels carefully.
On the mezzanine of the staircase hangs a painting of the baptism scene at "Calivo." It is based on the story of Legazpi's party and the Ati people in 1569.
This exhibit introduces the lives, food, art, local crafts and economy of the Aklan people. You can also see local culture such as Ati-Atihan costumes and piña cloth.

These cover Aklan natives such as Archbishop Gabriel Reyes, Cardinal Jaime Sin, Godofredo Ramos, and Gil Mijares and Pastor Martelino. Looking at one person at a time sorts out the region's modern history.

blocks.title: The origin of the name Kalibo

children.text: The most widely accepted explanation is that the name Kalibo comes from the Aklanon "sanka libo," meaning "one thousand." It links to the story of the mass baptism of the Ati people in 1569.

The plaza in front of the museum has statues of Rizal and Bonifacio, a historical marker for Gabriel Reyes (unveiled by the NHCP in March 2022), monuments to Mijares and Martelino, and a World War II veterans' obelisk.
At the town's tourist information desk you can ask about sights, places to eat and seasonal foods. The staff will sometimes take your photo in front of the pediment.
Check sights and opening hours at the tourist information desk and buy a museum ticket.
Go through the exhibits on the first and second floors one after another at an unhurried pace.
On the top floor, take a photo with the surviving pediment and flagpole.
Look around the statues and monuments in Pastrana Park.
See Kalibo Cathedral right behind, then have lunch near the market.
Opening days and hours differ by source, so check ahead by phone or on the Facebook page.
See Museo it Akean and Pastrana Park.
Walk to Kalibo Cathedral and the Aklan Freedom Shrine.
Have lunch at a restaurant downtown.
Take a tricycle to Bakhawan Eco-Park and walk the mangrove boardwalk.

The museum is said to be open only on weekdays, so plan a full day on a weekday. Bakhawan Eco-Park is cooler after 3 PM than at midday, so see the museum in the morning and go to the mangroves in the afternoon.
There are direct flights from Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Kalibo International Airport (KLO) taking about
1 hour
. Which airlines fly the route changes, so check when you book.
From the airport you can go to the town center by tricycle or taxi, and one guide says the airport is close enough that it takes about
10~15 minutes
One guide says it takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
from Caticlan, the gateway to Boracay, to Kalibo by bus or van. Before boarding, confirm that you can get off in downtown Kalibo (Poblacion).

items.title: On foot or by tricycle downtown

children.text: The museum is right next to Kalibo Cathedral, and Pastrana Park and the market are within walking distance. If your hotel is in the town center you can walk.
Shared and special tricycle fares differ, so agree on the fare before you ride.
The phone number is (036) 268 9260, and the official Facebook page is "Museo it Akean." Opening days and hours differ by source, so it is safest to confirm before your visit.
The museum is indoors, so you can visit all year, and it is a good alternative on a rainy day. If you want to combine it with a city walk, the dry season from November to May is easier.

During the January Ati-Atihan festival the town is very crowded and opening hours may change. On a weekday morning before or after the festival it is quieter, and festival dates change each year, so check the latest announcements.

The museum is in the middle of downtown Kalibo, with many places to stay nearby. Lodging clusters in Poblacion, where the church and park are, and along the road to the airport, so choose a hotel near the airport for an early flight and one in the center if you want to walk to the museum and the church. During the Ati-Atihan festival, lodging fills up months ahead, so reserve early. One guide says business hotels run about
a night and simple pensions and guesthouses about
, but prices vary greatly by season, so check the latest rates on a booking site. During the festival rates can double or triple.

You can taste Aklan local dishes near the market. Binakol, chicken simmered in coconut water, and inubaran, banana stem pith cooked in coconut milk, are the signature dishes. The Sunday market is known for snacks such as suman sa latik and maruya. No restaurant inside the museum was confirmed, so eat at restaurants around the market.
Ask at the tourist information desk first for a map and seasonal foods, which makes planning the day easier.
Exhibits are split between the first and second floors, so go through the first floor first and read the labels slowly for better understanding.
Staff sometimes take your photo in front of the pediment on the top floor, so ask.
Enter the church next door in clothing that covers your shoulders and knees.
It is said to be open only on weekdays, so on a weekend change your plan to focus on the church and the park.
If you bring ID, you can check whether you qualify for the student, senior or PWD discount.
The exhibit labels are organized by theme, so start with the themes that interest you and look at the rest if time remains.
Nearby Pastrana Park is pleasant for a walk around sunset and becomes a stage during festivals. The plaza stands where the town's main streets meet, so it is easy to get your bearings.
Opening days and hours differ by source. One says weekdays 8 AM to 4 PM, another says Tuesday to Sunday with a midday break, so be sure to confirm before you visit.
The building was badly damaged by an earthquake in the 1980s and only part of the original remains. Follow safety instructions.
Some exhibits also present old claims that scholars have shown to be fabricated, so read the explanations critically.
Hours may change on holidays and during events, so check before you go.
During the festival pickpockets increase, so keep your belongings secure.
Numbers such as the year the building was put up (1882 or 1822) differ by source, so go by the on-site signs.
The Aklan capital
Kalibo
, where the museum stands, also has a market, piña weaving workshops and a mangrove forest.
The
Ati-Atihan Festival
, which peaks around Pastrana Park every January, goes well with the costume exhibit at the museum.
Reached via Caticlan,
Boracay
is the best-known beach destination connected to Kalibo.
The cathedral and park right next to the museum are minutes away on foot.
